content.title: Mental Model
content.message: Think of goroutines as tasks on a to-do list, and the Go runtime as a smart assistant with a few workers (OS threads). The assistant assigns tasks efficiently, switching when one is waiting. You describe what needs doing; Go figures out how to do it efficiently.

content.text: Goroutines are powerful, but how do you wait for them to finish? The next section introduces sync.WaitGroup, a simple counter that lets you wait for multiple goroutines to complete.

In the previous section, we used time.Sleep to wait for goroutines. That's unreliable: you're guessing how long to wait. Too short, and goroutines get killed. Too long, and you waste time. WaitGroup solves this. It waits until all goroutines actually finish, no guessing needed. Use WaitGroup when you just need to know when goroutines are done. If goroutines need to send data back, use channels instead (covered in the next section).
How It Works

A WaitGroup is a counter that tracks running goroutines. Think of it like a checklist: you add items before starting work, check them off when done, and wait until everything is checked off. Add(n) adds n items to the list. Done() checks off one item. Wait() blocks until the list is empty.

content.code:
+-----------------------------------------------+
|                                               |
|  wg.Add(3)                 counter: 3         |
|                                               |
|  goroutine 1: wg.Done()    counter: 2         |
|  goroutine 2: wg.Done()    counter: 1         |
|  goroutine 3: wg.Done()    counter: 0         |
|                                               |
|  wg.Wait()    blocks until counter == 0       |
|               unblocks, main continues        |
|                                               |
+-----------------------------------------------+

content.text: Declaring a WaitGroup
You declare a WaitGroup using var. The zero value is ready to use, no initialization needed.

content.code: var wg sync.WaitGroup    // Ready to use, counter starts at 0

content.text: Basic Usage

Here's the fundamental pattern. Notice that Add() is called before starting the goroutine, and Done() is deferred inside the goroutine. The defer keyword schedules a function to run when the surrounding function returns. This ensures Done() is always called, even if the goroutine panics.

content.output:
$ go run basic_waitgroup.go
Goroutine 1 working...
Goroutine 2 working...
Goroutine 1 done
Goroutine 2 done
All goroutines finished!

content.text: Goroutine 2 finishes last because it sleeps longer (200ms vs 100ms). The order of 'working' messages may vary since goroutines start concurrently, but 'All goroutines finished!' always prints last because wg.Wait() blocks until both call Done().
The Three Methods
Batch Add Pattern
When starting multiple similar goroutines, you can add the total count at once. This is cleaner and slightly more efficient than adding one at a time.

content.output:
$ go run batch_add.go
Processing: fetch products
Processing: fetch users
Processing: fetch orders
All tasks complete

content.text: The output order varies because goroutines run concurrently. The key pattern here is calling wg.Add(len(tasks)) once before the loop rather than wg.Add(1) inside each iteration. Both work, but batch adding is cleaner when you know the count upfront.

content.title: Critical: Add() Must Happen Before go
content.message: Always call Add() before starting the goroutine. If you call Add() inside the goroutine, there's a race: Wait() might see zero before the goroutine has a chance to increment the counter, and your program continues prematurely.

content.text: Parallel File Processing

Processing 4 files one by one takes 400ms (100ms each). Processing them in parallel takes only 100ms because all 4 run at the same time. WaitGroup lets you start all goroutines and wait for all of them to finish.

content.output:
$ go run parallel_files.go
Processed: config.yaml
Processed: users.json
Processed: report.csv
Processed: data.xml
Total time: 101.5ms

content.text: Notice the output order is different from the code order. That's because goroutines run concurrently and finish in unpredictable order. The Go scheduler decides which goroutine runs when. But WaitGroup doesn't care about order. It just waits until all goroutines call Done(), regardless of which finishes first. All 4 files finish in about 100ms, not 400ms. That's the power of parallel processing with WaitGroup.
Passing WaitGroup to Functions
When you pass a WaitGroup to a function, you must pass a pointer. WaitGroup contains internal state that must not be copied.

content.title: Negative Counter Causes Panic
content.message: If you call Done() more times than Add(), the counter goes negative and the program panics. This usually means you have a logic error: either calling Done() twice or not calling Add() enough times. Use defer wg.Done() to ensure exactly one Done() per goroutine.

content.text: When to Use WaitGroup

Use WaitGroup when you need to wait for goroutines to finish but don't need to collect results from them. If goroutines need to send data back, use channels instead (covered in the next section). Here are common scenarios:
Scenario 1: Download Files (Don't Need Content)
You want to download multiple files to disk. You don't need the content in your program, just need to know when all downloads finish.

content.output:
$ go run download_files.go
Downloading image2.png...
Downloading image1.png...
Downloading image3.png...
Saved image2.png to disk
Saved image1.png to disk
Saved image3.png to disk
All downloads complete!

content.text: All three downloads start almost simultaneously and each takes 100ms. Because they run in parallel, total time is about 100ms, not 300ms. WaitGroup ensures we don't print 'All downloads complete!' until every file is saved.
Scenario 2: Fire-and-Forget Tasks
You want to send emails or log events in the background. You don't care about the result, just need to make sure they complete before the program exits.

Scenario 3: When NOT to Use WaitGroup
If you need to collect results from goroutines, WaitGroup alone is not enough. You need channels. This example shows the problem:

This code has a race condition. Here's what goes wrong: the line 'total += price' is not atomic. It actually does three steps: (1) read current value of total, (2) add price to it, (3) write the result back. When two goroutines do this at the same time, they might both read total as 0, both add their price, and both write back. One update gets lost. Expected total: 225 (100+50+75). Actual result: could be 100, 125, 150, or 225 depending on timing. WaitGroup only waits for goroutines to finish. It doesn't protect shared data. To collect results safely, use channels (covered in the next section).

content.title: Common Pattern
content.message: The most common WaitGroup pattern is: Add(n) once, start n goroutines in a loop, each with defer wg.Done(), then wg.Wait() after the loop. This handles the vast majority of use cases.

content.text: WaitGroups let you wait for goroutines to finish, but what if goroutines need to share data with each other? The next section introduces channels, Go's primary mechanism for communication between goroutines.

Channels are Go's primary mechanism for communication between goroutines. Think of a channel as a pipe: one goroutine puts a value in, another takes it out. Go has two types of channels: unbuffered channels (sender waits for receiver) and buffered channels (sender can queue values without waiting). This section covers unbuffered channels. Buffered channels are covered in the next section.

Channels provide both communication and synchronization. Without channels, you'd need locks (mutexes) to safely share data between goroutines, manually ensuring only one goroutine accesses data at a time. Channels handle this automatically: when you send a value, ownership transfers to the receiver. No locks needed.
Creating and Using Channels

Create a channel using `make()`, specifying the type of values it carries. Use the `<-` operator to send and receive. The arrow shows the direction data flows: `ch <- value` sends into the channel (arrow points toward channel), and `value := <-ch` receives from the channel (arrow points away from channel).

content.output:
$ go run channel_basics.go
42

content.text: The goroutine sends 42 into the channel, and main receives it. The send and receive happen almost simultaneously because the channel is unbuffered. The goroutine blocks on `ch <- 42` until main is ready to receive.
How Channels Work
A channel connects a sender and receiver. The sender puts a value in (`ch <- 42`), the value travels through the channel, and the receiver takes it out (`v := <-ch`).

The channel we created with `make(chan int)` is an unbuffered channel. It has no storage. The value passes directly from sender to receiver. If you send and no one is receiving, you block. If you receive and no one is sending, you block. This is how unbuffered channels synchronize goroutines: sender and receiver must meet at the channel to exchange the value.
Channels Block
This blocking behavior is crucial to understand for unbuffered channels. Sends block until someone receives. Receives block until someone sends. This is not a bug; it's how goroutines coordinate.

content.output:
$ go run channel_blocking.go
Waiting...
done

content.text: "Waiting..." prints immediately. Then main blocks on `<-ch` for 2 seconds until the goroutine sends "done". This demonstrates how channels synchronize goroutines: the receiver waits for the sender.

content.title: Deadlock on Single Goroutine
content.message: The `main()` function runs in a goroutine too (the main goroutine). Sending and receiving on the same goroutine causes a deadlock. Here's why: when you send (`ch <- 1`), the goroutine pauses and waits for a receiver. But the receive code (`<-ch`) is on the next line, which never executes because the goroutine is stuck waiting. It's waiting for itself, forever.

content.text: This code deadlocks because the send on line 4 waits for a receiver, but line 5 (the receiver) can't run until line 4 finishes:
Go detects this and crashes with a clear error:

content.code:
fatal error: all goroutines are asleep - deadlock!

goroutine 1 [chan send]:
main.main()
	deadlock_example.go:4 +0x38
exit status 2

content.text: The fix: sender and receiver must be in different goroutines. Move the send to a separate goroutine so the main goroutine can receive:

content.output:
$ go run deadlock_fix.go
1

content.text: Now it works. The send happens in a separate goroutine, so main can proceed to the receive. The two goroutines meet at the channel: one sends, one receives, value transfers.
Channels as Synchronization
Beyond passing data, channels synchronize goroutines. A common pattern is the signal channel: a channel used only to signal an event, not to pass meaningful data.

content.output:
$ go run signal_channel.go
Working...
Done!
Goroutine finished

content.text: The main goroutine blocks on `<-done` until the worker goroutine sends. This demonstrates using a channel purely for synchronization, not data. The empty struct value is just a token to unblock the receiver.

content.title: Why struct{}?
content.message: For signal channels, use `chan struct{}` instead of `chan bool`. An empty struct takes zero bytes of memory, making it clear this channel is for signaling, not data. The syntax `struct{}{}` looks odd: `struct{}` is the type (empty struct), and the second `{}` creates a value of that type. It's like how `int` is a type and `42` is a value.

content.text: When to Use Channels
Unbuffered channels are perfect for synchronization and signaling. Here are common patterns:
Graceful Shutdown

When your program needs to stop, you can't just kill goroutines. They might be in the middle of writing to a file or processing a request. Graceful shutdown means telling goroutines to finish what they're doing and exit cleanly. A signal channel solves this. You create an unbuffered channel and pass it to all goroutines. When it's time to stop, you close the channel. Closing broadcasts to all receivers at once: every goroutine waiting on that channel wakes up immediately. This is why unbuffered channels are perfect here. You don't need to send a value to each goroutine, just close once and everyone gets the signal.
Output (server order may vary):

content.code:
Server 1: handling request
Server 2: handling request
Server 3: handling request
Server 1: handling request
Server 2: handling request
Server 3: handling request
Main: sending shutdown signal
Server 1: shutting down
Server 3: shutting down
Server 2: shutting down

content.text: The shutdown channel uses struct{} because we don't need to send any data, just a signal. Closing the channel wakes up all goroutines waiting on it simultaneously.
Pipeline Processing

A pipeline is a chain of steps. Each step takes input, does one thing, and passes the output to the next step. Think of making a sandwich: one person slices bread, passes it to someone who adds filling, who passes it to someone who wraps it. Each person focuses on one task. In Go, each step is a goroutine. Channels connect the steps. Step 1 sends to a channel, Step 2 reads from that channel and sends to another, and so on. The best part: all steps run at the same time. While Step 3 wraps sandwich 1, Step 2 is filling sandwich 2, and Step 1 is slicing bread for sandwich 3.

Let's trace through: 1 goes in, gets squared to 1, then doubled to 2. Same for others: 2→4→8, 3→9→18, 4→16→32. All three stages run at the same time. While the double stage works on the first number, the square stage is already working on the second number.

Why unbuffered channels here? They create backpressure. Backpressure means 'slow down if the next step can't keep up.' If the double stage is slow, the square stage can't send its result until double is ready to receive. This automatically prevents fast stages from overwhelming slow ones. No data piles up, no memory grows out of control.
Channel Types
Channels can carry any type, including structs, pointers, and even other channels. Here are some examples of channel declarations:

content.text: Unbuffered channels are powerful but can be limiting. What if you want to send multiple values without blocking? The next section covers buffered channels, which add a queue between sender and receiver.

With unbuffered channels, a send blocks until another goroutine receives. What if your sender needs to keep working without waiting? Buffered channels can hold values until a receiver is ready. You can send multiple values without blocking, as long as the buffer isn't full. This lets sender and receiver work at their own pace.
Creating Buffered Channels
Pass a second argument to make() specifying the buffer size. A buffered channel can hold that many values before sends block.

content.output:
$ go run buffered_channel.go
1
2
3

content.text: All three sends complete without blocking because the buffer has room. The receives then drain the buffer in FIFO order. If we uncommented the fourth send, it would block forever since no goroutine is receiving.
How It Works

Think of an unbuffered channel as a direct handoff: the sender must wait for the receiver. A buffered channel has slots to hold values. The sender places values into the buffer, and the receiver takes them out in order (first in, first out).

content.code:
Unbuffered (capacity 0)              Buffered (capacity 3)

  +--------+       +--------+           +--------+ +---+---+---+ +--------+
  |  send  |------>|  recv  |           |  send  |>| 1 | 2 | 3 |>|  recv  |
  +--------+       +--------+           +--------+ +---+---+---+ +--------+

  Direct handoff                        Buffer holds up to 3 values
  (sender waits for receiver)           (sender and receiver independent)

content.text: When Buffered Channels Block

Buffered channels still block, just not as often. If you send and the buffer is full, your goroutine waits. If you receive and the buffer is empty, your goroutine waits. The buffer gives you room before blocking happens.

content.output:
$ go run buffered_blocking.go
1
2

content.text: With a buffer of 2, both sends succeed immediately. Both receives also succeed because data is available. The commented lines would cause deadlock: sending to a full buffer or receiving from an empty one blocks forever when there's no other goroutine to help.
When to Use Buffered Channels
Buffered channels shine in specific patterns. Here are the most common ones:
Worker Pool

A worker pool is a group of goroutines that process jobs from a shared queue. Instead of creating a new goroutine for every job, you reuse a fixed number of workers. This is more efficient because creating goroutines has overhead, and too many goroutines can exhaust memory. Think of a restaurant kitchen with 3 chefs. Orders come in and wait on a ticket rail. Each chef takes the next order when ready. If orders arrive faster than chefs can cook, orders queue up on the rail. In Go, a buffered channel is the ticket rail. Workers receive jobs from the channel. The buffer lets jobs queue up instead of blocking the sender.
Output (worker order may vary):

content.text: Notice all 9 jobs are sent immediately without blocking. The buffer (capacity 10) holds them until workers are ready. Three workers process jobs in parallel: while Worker 1 handles job 1, Workers 2 and 3 handle jobs 2 and 3. Each worker takes the next available job from the channel. When all jobs are sent, we close the channel. The 'range jobs' loop in each worker exits when the channel is closed and empty.

Why do we need WaitGroup here? The channel handles job distribution, but closing a channel doesn't mean workers are done. Closing only signals 'no more jobs will be sent.' Workers can still receive and process jobs that are already in the buffer. The 'range jobs' loop keeps receiving until the channel is both closed AND empty. After that, each worker might still be processing its last job. Without WaitGroup, main would exit immediately after close(jobs), killing workers mid-work. WaitGroup solves this: each worker calls Done() after finishing all its work. Main calls Wait() to block until all workers are truly done.
Async Logging

Async logging means writing log messages in the background instead of blocking your main code. Writing to disk or sending logs over a network is slow. If your app waits for each log write, it slows down. Async logging solves this by handing off log messages to a background worker. Think of leaving notes for an assistant: you write a quick note and continue working, while your assistant files it later. In Go, your app sends log messages to a buffered channel. A separate goroutine reads from the channel and writes logs at its own pace. Your app never waits.

content.text: Notice the app finishes all 5 events before any log is written. The app sends messages to the buffer and continues immediately. The background goroutine writes logs slowly (100ms each), but the app doesn't wait. The buffer (capacity 100) holds messages until the logger catches up.

Why use a 'done' channel instead of WaitGroup? Both work, but here we have only one goroutine. A channel is simpler for single goroutine: send a signal when done, receive to wait. WaitGroup is better when you have multiple goroutines to wait for. The 'done' channel also demonstrates that channels themselves can be used for synchronization, not just data transfer.
Rate Limiting

Rate limiting controls how many requests a system handles at once. Without limits, a sudden spike in traffic can crash your server or overwhelm a database. Rate limiting protects your system by making excess requests wait or rejecting them. Think of a doctor's office with a waiting room that holds 10 people. If 15 patients arrive, 5 must wait outside until someone leaves. In Go, a buffered channel acts as the waiting room. The buffer capacity is the maximum waiting requests. When full, new requests block until space opens up.

This is rate limiting through backpressure. When the system is overwhelmed, new requests naturally slow down because they block waiting for buffer space. The sender (incoming requests) can't outpace the receiver (handler) by more than the buffer size. In production, you might add a timeout: if a request can't be queued within N seconds, reject it with 'server too busy' instead of waiting forever.
Batch Processing

Batch processing means collecting multiple items and processing them together instead of one by one. This is faster because some operations have overhead: opening a database connection, making a network call, or writing to disk. Doing it once for 100 items is cheaper than doing it 100 times. Think of a mail carrier: delivering 50 letters in one trip is faster than making 50 separate trips. In Go, a buffered channel collects items. A goroutine reads from the channel, groups items into a batch, and processes the batch when full.

Why is batching faster? Imagine writing to a database. Each write has overhead: open connection, authenticate, execute, close. Writing 5 items one by one = 5x overhead. Writing 5 items in one batch = 1x overhead. The 'batch = batch[:0]' line resets the slice without allocating new memory. It keeps the underlying array but sets length to 0, ready for the next batch.
Semaphore Pattern

A semaphore is a counter that controls access to a shared resource. It tracks how many slots are available. When a goroutine wants access, it takes a slot. When done, it returns the slot. If no slots are available, the goroutine waits. Think of a swimming pool with 3 lanes: only 3 people can swim at once, and person 4 must wait until someone finishes. In Go, a buffered channel works as a semaphore. The buffer capacity is the number of slots. Sending takes a slot, receiving returns a slot. If the buffer is full, sending blocks until a slot opens.

content.text: Notice the pattern: only 3 workers run at the same time. Workers 1, 2, 3 start immediately. Worker 4 can't start until one of them finishes. When Worker 2 finishes and releases its slot, Worker 4 grabs it and starts. This continues until all 10 workers complete.

How does it work? The semaphore is a buffered channel with capacity 3. Sending to the channel (sem <- struct{}{}) acquires a slot. If 3 slots are taken, the send blocks. Receiving from the channel (<-sem) releases a slot, letting a waiting goroutine proceed. This pattern is useful for limiting concurrent access to databases, APIs, file handles, or any resource that can't handle unlimited parallel requests.
Pub/Sub Within Service

Pub/Sub (publish-subscribe) lets one publisher send events to multiple subscribers. Each subscriber has its own channel and processes events independently. The publisher doesn't need to know how many subscribers exist or how fast they process. Think of a news broadcast: the station sends once, and every TV tuned in receives it. In Go, each subscriber gets a buffered channel. The publisher sends to all channels. Buffering is important here because slow subscribers shouldn't block the publisher or other subscribers.
Output (subscriber order may vary):

Subscriber 1 received: event-1
Subscriber 2 received: event-1
Subscriber 3 received: event-1
Subscriber 1 received: event-2
Subscriber 2 received: event-2
Subscriber 3 received: event-2

content.text: Each subscriber receives both events. The publisher sends once, and all 3 subscribers get the message. This is fan-out: one input becomes multiple outputs. Each subscriber has its own buffered channel (capacity 10), so they process independently.

Why buffered channels? Without buffers, the publisher would block on each subscriber. If Subscriber 1 is slow, Subscribers 2 and 3 wait too. With buffers, the publisher sends to all channels quickly and continues. Each subscriber processes at its own pace.

What is sync.RWMutex? A mutex (mutual exclusion) prevents multiple goroutines from accessing shared data at the same time. RWMutex is a special mutex with two modes: read lock (RLock) and write lock (Lock). Multiple goroutines can hold read locks simultaneously because reading doesn't change data. But a write lock is exclusive: only one goroutine can hold it, and no readers allowed. In our PubSub, Publish only reads the subscriber list (uses RLock), so multiple Publish calls can run in parallel. Subscribe and Close modify the list (use Lock), so they block everything else. This gives us both safety and performance.
Choosing Buffer Size
Buffer size is a design decision, not an afterthought. Too small and you get unnecessary blocking. Too large and you waste memory and hide backpressure problems.

items.description: Forces synchronization. Use when sender should wait for receiver to be ready.

items.label: Buffer Size 1
items.description: Allows sender to 'fire and continue' for one item. Common for signal channels.

items.label: Buffer Size N
items.description: Absorbs bursts up to N items. Set based on expected burst size or worker count.

content.title: Large Buffers Hide Problems
content.message: A huge buffer (like 10,000) can mask a slow consumer. The producer happily fills the buffer while memory grows. Then when the buffer fills, everything suddenly blocks. Prefer smaller buffers that surface backpressure early: when the buffer fills, the sender blocks, signaling that the consumer can't keep up.

package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	ch := make(chan int, 5)
	
	ch <- 1
	ch <- 2
	
	fmt.Println("Length:", len(ch))   // 2 (items in buffer)
	fmt.Println("Capacity:", cap(ch)) // 5 (buffer size)
}

$ go run len_cap.go

content.text: After sending 2 values to a channel with capacity 5, len() returns 2 (items currently buffered) and cap() returns 5 (maximum buffer size). These functions let you inspect channel state, but be careful using them for control flow.

content.title: Don't Rely on len() for Synchronization
content.message: Checking len(ch) before sending is a race condition. Between checking and sending, another goroutine might send. Use select with default for non-blocking sends instead (covered in the select section).

content.text: Quick Reference

So far, channels can both send and receive. But what if you want to restrict a function to only sending or only receiving? The next section covers directional channels, which add type safety to channel operations.

By default, channels are bidirectional: you can both send and receive. Go lets you restrict channels to send-only or receive-only in function parameters. This adds type safety and makes the code's intent clear.

Think of a one-way street: traffic flows in only one direction. A send-only channel is like an entrance ramp where you can only put cars onto the road. A receive-only channel is like an exit ramp where you can only take cars off. This restriction prevents accidents: you cannot accidentally drive the wrong way.

content.code:
Bidirectional (chan T)         Send-only (chan<- T)        Receive-only (<-chan T)

       +-----+                        +-----+                       +-----+
  -->  |     |  -->               --> |     |                       |     |  -->
       | ch  |                        | ch  |                       | ch  |
  <--  |     |  <--                   |     |                       |     |
       +-----+                        +-----+                       +-----+

  Can send AND receive            Can ONLY send               Can ONLY receive

content.code:
chan T      // Bidirectional: can send and receive
chan<- T    // Send-only: can only send
<-chan T    // Receive-only: can only receive

content.text: The arrow shows what you can do: chan<- means data goes into the channel (send), <-chan means data comes out (receive).
Using Directional Channels in Functions
The common pattern is to create a bidirectional channel, then pass it to functions with restricted access. This prevents bugs where a function accidentally sends when it should only receive.

content.output:
$ go run directional_example.go
Received: 0
Received: 1
Received: 2
Received: 3
Received: 4

content.text: The producer sends values 0-4 into the channel and closes it when done. The consumer receives each value and prints it. Notice how the bidirectional channel ch is automatically converted to send-only (chan<-) when passed to producer and receive-only (<-chan) when passed to consumer.

content.title: Automatic Conversion
content.message: A bidirectional channel automatically converts to a directional channel when passed to a function. You don't need explicit casts. The reverse (directional to bidirectional) is not allowed.

content.title: Conversion is One-Way
content.message: A bidirectional channel can become directional, but not the reverse. Once you have a <-chan or chan<-, you cannot convert it back to chan. This is intentional: it prevents functions from gaining more access than they were given.

content.text: Why Use Directional Channels?

rows: Wrong operation causes compile error, not runtime bug
Function signature documents whether it sends or receives
Can't accidentally close a receive-only channel
Public APIs can expose limited channel access

content.text: The compiler tells you exactly what went wrong: the operation (send or receive) is invalid because the channel type doesn't allow it. Notice how the error includes both the variable name and its type, making it easy to trace the issue back to the function signature.
Closing Directional Channels
Only the sender should close a channel. Go enforces this: you can close a send-only (chan<-) channel but not a receive-only (<-chan) channel.
Generator Function
A generator creates a channel, starts a goroutine that sends values, and returns a receive-only channel. The caller can only receive, protecting the channel from misuse.

content.output:
$ go run generator.go
0
1
2
3
4

content.text: The Generate function creates a bidirectional channel internally but returns it as receive-only (<-chan int). This means callers can only read from it, not send. The goroutine inside Generate owns the channel and closes it when done. This pattern is common for streaming data: the generator controls the channel lifetime while consumers can only receive.
Quick Reference

You now know how to create, buffer, and restrict channels. But what happens when you close a channel? The next section covers closing channels, range loops over channels, and the patterns that emerge from channel closure.
Closing a channel signals that no more values will be sent. This is how a sender tells receivers that work is done. Understanding channel closure is essential for writing correct concurrent programs.
How to Close a Channel

content.code:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	ch := make(chan int, 3)
	
	ch <- 1
	ch <- 2
	ch <- 3
	close(ch) // No more sends allowed
	
	// Receives still work - drain buffered values
	fmt.Println(<-ch) // 1
	fmt.Println(<-ch) // 2
	fmt.Println(<-ch) // 3
	fmt.Println(<-ch) // 0 (zero value, channel closed and empty)
}

content.output:
$ go run close_channel.go
1
2
3
0

content.text: After close() is called, no more values can be sent, but buffered values can still be received. Once the buffer is empty, subsequent receives return the zero value (0 for int). The channel remains in the closed state permanently.
Detecting Closed Channels
A receive from a closed channel returns the zero value immediately. To distinguish between a real zero value and a closed channel, use the two-value receive form.

content.code:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	ch := make(chan int, 2)
	ch <- 0 // Sending actual zero
	close(ch)
	
	// Two-value receive: value and ok
	v1, ok1 := <-ch
	fmt.Println(v1, ok1) // 0 true (real value)
	
	v2, ok2 := <-ch
	fmt.Println(v2, ok2) // 0 false (channel closed)
}

content.output:
$ go run detect_closed.go
0 true
0 false

content.text: The two-value receive form returns the value and a boolean indicating whether the channel is open. When ok is true, the value is real. When ok is false, the channel is closed and empty, and the value is the zero value. This is how you distinguish between a sent zero and a closed channel.
Range Over Channels
The range loop automatically receives values until the channel is closed. This is the cleanest way to consume all values from a channel.

content.output:
$ go run range_channel.go
0
1
2
3
4
Channel closed, loop ended

content.text: The range loop receives values 0 through 4, then detects the channel closure and exits. This is equivalent to repeatedly calling the two-value receive and checking the ok boolean, but much cleaner. The goroutine sends five values, closes the channel, and terminates.

content.title: Forgetting to Close
content.message: If you use range over a channel and never close it, the loop blocks forever waiting for more values. This is a common source of goroutine leaks. Always close channels when done sending.

content.text: Rules of Channel Closure

content.code:
// These cause panics:

ch := make(chan int)
close(ch)

ch <- 1    // PANIC: send on closed channel
close(ch)  // PANIC: close of closed channel

content.text: Who Should Close?
Only the sender should close a channel. The receiver has no way to know if more values are coming. If a receiver closes the channel, the sender will panic when it tries to send.

items.label: Sender Closes
items.description: Correct. Sender knows when it's done. Receivers detect closure via range or ok check.

items.label: Receiver Closes
items.description: Wrong. Sender will panic on next send. Use a separate 'done' channel to signal cancellation.

content.text: All three workers block on receiving from the start channel. After a one-second delay, closing the channel unblocks all of them simultaneously. The order workers print may vary between runs, but they all start at the same moment. This pattern is often called the 'starting gun' or 'barrier' pattern.

content.title: Close for Broadcast
content.message: Closing a channel is the only way to wake up multiple receivers simultaneously. Sending a value wakes up only one receiver. This makes close() perfect for cancellation signals and 'starting gun' patterns.

content.text: What if you need to receive from multiple channels? Or send to whichever channel is ready first? The next section covers the select statement, Go's multiplexer for channel operations.

The select statement lets a goroutine wait on multiple channel operations. It's like a switch statement, but for channels. Select blocks until one of its cases can proceed, then executes that case. If multiple cases are ready, it picks one randomly.
Basic select

content.code: from ch1

content.text: The select statement does not wait for all channels. It blocks until exactly one case becomes ready, executes that case, and then finishes. Here, ch1 receives first (100ms vs 200ms), so that case runs and the program exits. The ch2 goroutine is still running, but no one receives its message.
First Ready Wins

content.code:
select {
    case <-ch1:    --+
        ...          |
    case <-ch2:    --+-- One case becomes ready
        ...          |    v
    case ch3 <- v: --+    Execute that case
        ...              (random if multiple ready)
    }

content.text: Timeouts with select

Remember, select blocks until one case is ready. What if an operation takes too long? Without a timeout, your program waits forever. The time.After function returns a channel that receives a value after the specified duration. By combining it with select, you create a race: either the result arrives first, or the timeout fires first. Whichever happens first wins.

content.output:
$ go run select_timeout.go
Timeout!

content.text: The operation takes 2 seconds, but we only wait 1 second. The time.After case fires first, so we print 'Timeout!' and exit. The goroutine sending to ch continues running in the background, but the buffered channel lets it complete without blocking forever.

content.title: Prevent Goroutine Leaks with Buffered Channels
content.message: When using select with timeouts, use a buffered channel (capacity 1) so the sending goroutine can complete even if the timeout fires first. With an unbuffered channel, the goroutine would block forever trying to send.

content.text: Non-blocking Operations with default

Sometimes you want to check a channel without waiting. Adding a default case makes select non-blocking: if no channel is ready, select runs the default case immediately instead of blocking. Think of it as 'try to receive, but don't wait if nothing is there.'

content.output:
$ go run select_default.go
No value available
Channel not ready

content.text: Both operations fall through to default because the channel is unbuffered and empty. The receive finds no value waiting, and the send finds no receiver waiting. Without default, both selects would block forever. The default case makes these checks instantaneous.

content.text: Let's see each pattern in action.
Timeout

Waiting forever is dangerous. A slow server, a network hiccup, or a stuck database can freeze your entire program. Timeouts let you say 'I'll wait this long, but no longer.' Think of ordering food at a restaurant: if your meal doesn't arrive in 30 minutes, you might leave. In Go, time.After creates a channel that receives after a duration. Put it in a select alongside your real work. Whichever happens first wins.

content.code:
Fetching data...
Timeout: server too slow

content.text: The server takes 3 seconds, but we only wait 1 second. The timeout fires first, so we print the timeout message and move on. The slow goroutine continues running in the background, but we don't wait for it. Notice the buffered channel (capacity 1): this prevents a goroutine leak when the timeout fires.
Cancellation

Users close browser tabs. Clients disconnect. Requests get cancelled. Your code needs to stop work when this happens, not keep burning CPU on something nobody wants anymore. The context package is Go's standard way to handle cancellation. A context has a Done() channel that closes when cancellation is requested. Think of a waiter who checks if the customer is still at the table before bringing each course. In Go, your select listens for both the result and the cancellation signal.

content.code: Cancelled: context deadline exceeded

content.text: The work takes 500ms, but the context times out after 200ms. The ctx.Done() case fires first, returning an error. In HTTP handlers, the context comes from the request and cancels automatically when the client disconnects. Always pass context to functions that do slow work, and always check ctx.Done() in your select.
First Response Wins

Sometimes you have multiple ways to get the same data: replicated databases, CDN edge servers, or redundant APIs. Instead of picking one and hoping it's fast, query them all and use whichever responds first. This is called 'hedging' or 'racing.' Think of sending three couriers to fetch a document: you use whichever courier returns first. In Go, start a goroutine for each source, and select on all their channels.

content.code: response from server-B

content.text: Server-B responds in 100ms, beating Server-C (200ms) and Server-A (300ms). We get Server-B's response and ignore the others. The other goroutines keep running and eventually send to their channels, but nobody receives. The buffered channels (capacity 1) let them complete without blocking forever.
Fan-in

Fan-in means combining multiple input streams into one. You have several producers sending data, and you want one consumer to handle all of it. Think of a call center: multiple phone lines ring, but one operator answers whichever rings first. In Go, you select on multiple channels and process whichever has data. This merges the streams into a single flow.

content.text: Both producers send messages at roughly the same time. The select picks whichever is ready, interleaving messages from both sources. The consumer doesn't need to know how many producers exist. It just keeps receiving until it has all 4 messages. You can use a nil channel pattern (covered later) to handle producers that close at different times.
Heartbeat

Long operations need signs of life. Users want to know something is happening. Network connections need keepalive signals. A heartbeat sends periodic messages while waiting for the main work to complete. Think of a loading spinner: it doesn't mean the work is faster, but it tells you the app isn't frozen. In Go, use a Ticker alongside your work channel. The select handles whichever fires.

content.text: The ticker fires every 500ms, printing 'still working...' three times during the 2-second wait. When the work finally completes, that case fires, we print the result and return. Always call ticker.Stop() when done to free resources. The defer ensures this happens even if we return early.
select in a Loop

A single select runs once and exits. But most concurrent programs need to handle events continuously: new messages arrive, timers fire, cancellation signals come in. Wrapping select in a for loop creates an event loop that keeps processing events until told to stop. Think of a receptionist at a desk: they don't handle one phone call and go home. They keep answering calls, greeting visitors, and checking emails in a loop, until their shift ends.

When the done signal arrives, we stop the ticker and return, breaking out of the loop. Without the return statement, the loop would continue forever.

content.title: Busy Loop with Default
content.message: Putting select with default in a tight loop creates a busy loop that wastes CPU. Use default only when you have other work to do between checks, not just to avoid blocking.

content.text: Multiple Ready Cases

What happens when two channels are ready at the exact same moment? If select always picked the first case, that channel would get priority and the second channel might never be served. This is called starvation. To prevent it, Go's select uses pseudo-random selection when multiple cases are ready. Think of a coin flip: if two people arrive at a door simultaneously, you flip a coin to decide who goes first. Over many iterations, both get roughly equal turns.
Output (varies each run):

Each iteration fills both channels, then selects from them. Since both are ready, Go randomly picks one. Run it multiple times and you'll get different sequences. Over many runs, you'll see roughly equal distribution of 1s and 2s. This randomness is intentional: it guarantees fairness and prevents bugs where one channel dominates.
Quick Reference
Select handles nil channels in a special way: cases with nil channels are skipped. This enables powerful patterns for dynamic channel management, covered in the next section.

A nil channel is a channel that hasn't been initialized with make(). Operations on nil channels behave differently than on regular channels: sends and receives block forever, and select ignores nil cases. This seemingly odd behavior enables elegant dynamic patterns.
nil Channel Behavior

content.output:
$ go run nil_channel.go
default runs

content.text: Since ch is nil, the case <-ch is skipped entirely. The select falls through to the default case and prints "default runs". Without the default, the select would block forever because the nil channel case can never be ready.
Why Is This Useful?
The key insight is that nil channels in select are ignored. You can dynamically enable or disable select cases by setting channels to nil.
Disable After First Receive

A common pattern is receiving from a channel once, then setting it to nil so subsequent selects skip it. Think of it like a checklist: once you've checked off an item, you don't need to look at it again. By setting a channel to nil after receiving, you're telling select to ignore that case from now on.

This is useful when you need to collect exactly one value from multiple sources, like waiting for the first response from several services, or gathering one-time configuration from different providers.

content.output:
$ go run disable_case.go
one
two

content.text: In iteration 1, select picks one of the ready channels (say ch1), prints "one", and sets ch1 = nil. In iteration 2, the ch1 case is now skipped because it's nil, so select receives from ch2, prints "two", and sets ch2 = nil. Without the nil trick, select might try to receive from an already-drained buffered channel and block forever.
Merge Channels Until Both Closed

Fan-in is a common concurrency pattern where multiple input channels are merged into a single output channel. Think of it like a funnel: several streams of data flow into one pipe. The challenge is knowing when to stop. You can't just loop forever because you need to close the output channel when all inputs are done.

The nil channel trick solves this elegantly. When an input channel closes, set it to nil. The loop condition `ch1 != nil || ch2 != nil` keeps running as long as at least one channel is still active. When both are nil, the loop exits and the output channel closes.

(order may vary)

content.text: The output order is non-deterministic because both producer goroutines run concurrently. The key behavior is that all 6 values appear exactly once, and the program terminates cleanly. When ch1 closes, its case returns ok=false, so we set ch1=nil. Select then only considers ch2 until it also closes. Once both are nil, the loop exits, close(out) runs via defer, and the range in main() completes.
Optional Channel

Sometimes a feature is optional. For example, a worker might support cancellation, but not all callers need it. Instead of requiring every caller to create a cancel channel, you can make it optional by accepting a nil channel.

Think of it like a light switch that may or may not be installed. If there's no switch (nil), the select simply ignores that case. If a switch exists (non-nil channel), the select listens for it. This lets you write one worker implementation that handles both scenarios.

$ go run optional_channel.go
Processing job 1
Processing job 2

content.text: The worker has a cancel field, but we pass nil. Inside Run(), the select has a case for <-w.cancel, but since cancel is nil, that case is permanently skipped. The worker only processes jobs until the jobs channel closes. If we passed a real cancel channel instead, closing it would trigger early termination. Same code, different behavior based on whether the channel is nil or not.

content.title: Don't Confuse nil and Closed
content.message: A nil channel blocks forever; a closed channel returns immediately. Setting ch = nil disables a select case. Receiving from closed returns zero values. These are very different behaviors.

content.text: Quick Reference

Channels provide communication, but when multiple goroutines need to access shared memory, you need protection against race conditions. The next section covers Mutexes, Go's tool for safe concurrent access to shared data.

A mutex (mutual exclusion lock) protects shared data from concurrent access. When multiple goroutines read and write the same variable without coordination, you get a race condition: unpredictable behavior that depends on timing. Mutexes ensure that only one goroutine accesses the critical section at a time.
Why Concurrent Access Breaks Things

Imagine a bank account with $100. You and your partner both try to withdraw $80 at the same time from different locations. Both transactions check the balance: $100. Both see enough money. Both approve the withdrawal. Both update the balance to $20. The bank just gave out $160 from a $100 account. This is a race condition.

The same thing happens in Go. When you write counter++, it looks like one operation, but it's actually three steps: read the current value, add one to it, write the new value back. If two goroutines run counter++ at the same time, they can both read the same value before either writes. One update gets lost.

content.code: Counter: 947

content.text: We started 1000 goroutines, each adding 1 to the counter. The result should be 1000, but it's less. Run it again and you'll get a different number: 983, 961, 1000, or something else. The result is unpredictable because goroutines are racing to update the same variable.

content.code:
Race Condition: Lost Update

    Time    Goroutine A         Goroutine B         counter
    ---------------------------------------------------------
    1       read counter (5)                        5
    2                           read counter (5)    5
    3       add 1 -> 6                              5
    4                           add 1 -> 6          5
    5       write 6                                 6
    6                           write 6             6  <- Lost!

    Both incremented, but counter only went from 5 to 6, not 7

content.text: Fixing It With sync.Mutex
The fix is simple: make goroutines take turns. A Mutex (short for "mutual exclusion") is like a lock on a door. Only one goroutine can hold the lock at a time. Others must wait.

It has two methods: Lock() takes the lock. If another goroutine already has it, you wait. Unlock() releases the lock so someone else can take it. The code between Lock() and Unlock() is called the "critical section", only one goroutine runs it at a time.

content.code: Counter: 1000

content.text: Run this code as many times as you want. The answer is always 1000. When goroutine A calls Lock(), goroutine B has to wait. B can't read the counter until A finishes updating and calls Unlock(). No more two goroutines reading the same value. No more lost updates.
Mental Model: A Room With One Key

Think of a mutex as a room with a single key hanging outside. To enter (access shared data), you take the key (Lock). While you have the key, no one else can enter. When you leave, you hang the key back (Unlock) so someone else can enter.

content.code:
Mutex as a Single-Key Room

    +----------------------------------------------+
    |  [Key] hangs here when room is available     |
    |                                              |
    |  +------------------------------------+      |
    |  |  Critical Section (shared data)    |      |
    |  |                                    |      |
    |  |  Only 1 goroutine at a time        |      |
    |  +------------------------------------+      |
    |                                              |
    |  G1: Lock() -> takes key, enters             |
    |  G2: Lock() -> no key, waits outside         |
    |  G1: Unlock() -> hangs key, leaves           |
    |  G2: takes key, enters                       |
    +----------------------------------------------+

content.text: Always Use defer Unlock()
The most important mutex pattern: immediately defer the Unlock after Lock. This guarantees Unlock runs even if your code panics, preventing deadlocks.

content.title: Forgetting Unlock Causes Deadlock
content.message: If you call Lock() but never Unlock(), all other goroutines waiting for that mutex will block forever. This is called a deadlock. Always use defer mu.Unlock() immediately after mu.Lock() to prevent this.

content.text: Protecting Struct Fields
So far we protected a simple variable. But what if you have a struct with multiple fields? Put the mutex inside the struct. Now the lock and the data it protects stay together.

Then create methods like Increment() and Value() that handle locking internally. Anyone using your struct just calls these methods. They don't need to worry about Lock() and Unlock(). The struct takes care of its own safety.

content.code: Counter: 1000

content.text: Notice how the main function doesn't call Lock() or Unlock() anywhere. The goroutines just call counter.Increment(). Inside that method, the mutex does its job: lock, update count, unlock. The caller doesn't see any of that. This pattern keeps your code simple and prevents mistakes like forgetting to unlock.
RWMutex: Multiple Readers, One Writer
A regular Mutex is strict: only one goroutine at a time, period. But reading data doesn't change it. Why make readers wait for each other?

sync.RWMutex is smarter. It has two modes: read mode and write mode. Multiple goroutines can read at the same time. But when someone needs to write, everyone else waits. Think of a notice board: anyone can read the notices at the same time. But when someone pins a new notice, others step back and wait until they're done.
Use RLock() and RUnlock() for reading. Use Lock() and Unlock() for writing.

The order is random because they run concurrently. If any goroutine called Set() during this time, all readers would wait until the write finished.
When to Use Mutex vs RWMutex

content.message: Use sync.Mutex first. Only switch to RWMutex if profiling shows read contention is a bottleneck. RWMutex has slightly higher overhead, so it only helps when you have many concurrent readers.

content.text: Mutex vs Channel: When to Use Each
Go's proverb says "share memory by communicating," but mutexes are still the right choice sometimes. Here's how to decide.
Common Mistakes
Finding Race Conditions: The -race Flag

Race conditions are hard to find by reading code. They depend on timing, so the bug might not show up every time you run the program. Go has a built-in race detector that watches your program as it runs and reports when two goroutines access the same variable without proper synchronization.
Add the -race flag to any Go command. It slows down your program but catches races that would otherwise hide.

content.code:
# Run your program with race detection
go run -race main.go

# Run tests with race detection
go test -race ./...

content.text: If the detector finds a race, it prints exactly where the problem is:

Write at 0x00c000014088 by goroutine 7:
  main.main.func1()
      /path/main.go:15 +0x38
-----
Previous write at 0x00c000014088 by goroutine 6:
  main.main.func1()
      /path/main.go:15 +0x38

content.text: This tells you: two goroutines (6 and 7) both wrote to the same memory address, and it happened at line 15 in main.go. Now you know exactly where to add a mutex.

content.title: Race Detector in CI
content.message: Run go test -race in your CI pipeline. The race detector has ~10x overhead, so don't use it in production, but it should be part of every test run.

content.text: Mutexes protect shared state, and WaitGroups wait for completion, but what about cancellation and timeouts? When a user cancels a request, how do you tell all the goroutines to stop? The next section covers the context package, Go's solution for cancellation and request-scoped data.

The context package provides a way to carry deadlines, cancellation signals, and request-scoped values across API boundaries and between goroutines. When a user cancels a request, you want all downstream operations (database queries, API calls, goroutines) to stop immediately. Context makes this possible.
Why Context Exists

Imagine an HTTP request that triggers multiple goroutines: one fetches from a database, another calls an external API, a third processes data. If the user closes their browser, all that work is wasted. Without context, those goroutines keep running. With context, you can cancel them all at once.

content.code:
Request Cancellation Without Context

    User cancels    Handler     DB Query    API Call    Processing
    -------------------------------------------------------------

                                (wasted)    (wasted)    (wasted)

    Request Cancellation With Context

    User cancels    Handler     DB Query    API Call    Processing
    -------------------------------------------------------------
         X ------> cancel() --> stops      stops       stops
                   propagates   (via ctx)  (via ctx)   (via ctx)

Context is an interface with four methods. Most of the time you only use Deadline(), Done(), and Err().

content.text: Creating Contexts

Contexts form a tree. Every context has a parent, except for the root. You start with one of two root contexts: Background() for normal operations, or TODO() as a placeholder when you're not sure which context to use yet.

From these roots, you create child contexts with added behavior: timeouts, cancellation, or attached values. When a parent is cancelled, all its children are cancelled too. This is how cancellation flows through your program.
WithCancel: Manual Cancellation

WithCancel creates a child context that you can cancel manually. It returns two things: the new context and a cancel function. Pass the context to your goroutines. When you want them to stop, call cancel().

Inside each goroutine, use select to watch ctx.Done(). This channel stays open while work should continue. When you call cancel(), the channel closes, and the select case triggers. That's the signal to clean up and return.

content.text: Both workers receive the same context. When cancel() is called, both see their ctx.Done() channel close and exit cleanly. One function call stopped two goroutines.

content.title: Always Call cancel()
content.message: WithCancel, WithTimeout, and WithDeadline all return a cancel function. Always call it when done, even if the context times out. This releases resources. Use defer cancel() immediately after creating the context.

content.text: WithTimeout: Automatic Cancellation
WithTimeout cancels the context automatically after a duration. Perfect for API calls that shouldn't hang forever.

content.output:
$ go run context_timeout.go

content.text: The operation needs 5 seconds to complete, but the context only allows 2 seconds. When the timeout expires, ctx.Done() closes and slowOperation returns the deadline exceeded error. This pattern is essential for preventing hung requests.
WithDeadline: Absolute Time Limit
WithTimeout says "cancel after 5 seconds from now." WithDeadline says "cancel at 3:00 PM." Use WithDeadline when you have a specific point in time, like an SLA deadline or a scheduled event.
You can check the deadline using ctx.Deadline(). It returns the time and a boolean (false if no deadline is set). This is useful when you need to set a shorter deadline for a sub-operation.

content.text: The work needs 2 seconds, but the deadline is only 1 second away. The context cancels at the deadline time, ctx.Done() closes, and doWork returns the error. The actual time in the output will match when you run it.
HTTP Handler with Database

This is where context shines. Every HTTP request in Go comes with a context (r.Context()). This context is cancelled automatically when the client disconnects. If you pass this context to your database calls, they stop too.

The pattern is: get the request's context, optionally add a timeout for extra protection, then pass it to every function that does I/O. The database driver, HTTP client, and other libraries all understand context and will stop their work when it's cancelled.

Three things can cancel this context: the client disconnects (r.Context() cancels), the 5-second timeout passes (WithTimeout cancels), or the server shuts down. In all cases, the database query stops immediately instead of wasting resources on a response nobody will receive.
Propagating Context Through Call Chain
Context should be passed as the first parameter to every function that does I/O or spawns goroutines. This creates a cancellation tree: cancelling a parent cancels all children.
WithValue: Request-Scoped Data

Sometimes you need to pass data that every function in the chain should have access to, but adding it as a parameter everywhere would be messy. Examples: request IDs for logging, authenticated user info, or tracing spans.

WithValue attaches a key-value pair to a context. Any function that receives this context can retrieve the value. But there's a catch: keys are compared using ==, so two packages using the string "userID" as a key would collide. The solution is to define your own unexported type for keys.

[req-12345] Processing order
[req-12345] Handler done

content.text: The request ID flows through every function without being passed as a parameter. This is useful for logging, tracing, and debugging. Every log line includes the request ID, making it easy to follow a single request through your system.

content.title: Don't Abuse context.Value
content.message: Only use context.Value for request-scoped data like request IDs, auth tokens, or tracing info. Don't use it to pass function parameters or dependencies. If a function needs data to do its job, make it an explicit parameter. The compiler can't check context values, so bugs are hard to find.

content.text: With context, you can now build production-ready concurrent programs that handle cancellation gracefully. Combined with goroutines, channels, WaitGroups, and Mutexes, you have Go's complete concurrency toolkit. The following sections cover common patterns that combine these primitives: worker pools, pipelines, and more.

When two goroutines try to increment the same counter, updates can get lost. One goroutine reads 5, adds 1 to get 6, but before it can write 6 back, another goroutine also reads 5 and writes 6. Two increments happened, but the counter only went up by 1.

Atomic operations solve this. They read, modify, and write a value in one step that cannot be interrupted. No other goroutine can sneak in between. The sync/atomic package provides these operations for counters, flags, and pointers.
The Problem with counter++
counter++ looks like one operation, but it's actually three: read the value, add 1, write the result. When goroutines run these steps at the same time, they can overwrite each other's work.

Non-Atomic: counter++ (3 separate operations)

    Goroutine A          Goroutine B         Memory
    -------------------------------------------------
    Read counter (5)                         5
                         Read counter (5)    5
    Add 1 = 6                                5
                         Add 1 = 6           5
    Write 6                                  6
                         Write 6             6  <- Lost update!

    Atomic: atomic.AddInt64 (single operation)

    Goroutine A          Goroutine B         Memory
    -------------------------------------------------
    AtomicAdd(1)                             5 -> 6
                         AtomicAdd(1)        6 -> 7  <- Correct!

content.text: The sync/atomic Package
The sync/atomic package provides five main operations for integers and pointers. Each operation works on pointers to the value, ensuring the operation happens directly in memory.

rows: Atomically add a delta to the value
Atomically replace and get old value

After Add(5): 15

Swap returned: 100
New value: 200

content.text: Each operation takes a pointer to the variable (&counter) and works directly on that memory location. Here's what each one does:
Add adds a number and returns the new value. Use it for counters. You can subtract by adding a negative number: atomic.AddInt64(&counter, -1).
Load reads the current value safely. Use it when you need to check a value that other goroutines might be changing.
Store writes a new value. Use it to set flags or reset counters.
Swap writes a new value and returns the old one. Use it when you need to know what value you replaced.

CompareAndSwap (CAS) is the most powerful. It only updates the value if it currently equals what you expect. If another goroutine changed it first, CAS fails and returns false. This lets you retry with the new value instead of blindly overwriting.
Go 1.19+ Atomic Types

The old-style functions like atomic.AddInt64(&counter, 1) have two problems. First, you must remember to pass a pointer. Second, nothing stops you from accidentally reading counter directly without atomic.Load, which creates a race condition.

Go 1.19 introduced typed wrappers that solve both problems. Instead of a raw int64, you declare an atomic.Int64. All operations are methods, so you can't forget the pointer. And you can't read the value without calling Load(), so accidental non-atomic reads are impossible.

content.text: atomic.Int64 is for counters and IDs. atomic.Bool is perfect for shutdown flags and feature toggles. atomic.Pointer[T] lets you swap entire structs atomically, which is useful for configuration that can change at runtime. The old config stays valid until all goroutines using it are done.
Concurrent Counter
Here's a practical example of a metrics counter used by an HTTP server. Multiple goroutines can safely increment counters without any locking.

Requests: 1000, Errors: 100

content.text: The numbers add up correctly: 1000 total requests, 100 errors (IDs 0, 10, 20, ... 990), 900 successful requests each with 100 bytes in (90,000 total) and 500 bytes out (450,000 total). All 1000 goroutines updated these counters at the same time, and no updates were lost.

Without atomic operations, some increments would be lost due to race conditions. With atomic, every Add() is guaranteed to work, no matter how many goroutines call it simultaneously. This pattern is common in web servers, load balancers, and monitoring dashboards.
Atomic vs Mutex: When to Use Each

Atomic operations are faster because they don't require locking. But they only work on single values. If you need to update two fields together (like transferring money from balance to pending), atomic can't help. By the time you update the second field, another goroutine might have read an inconsistent state.
Here's the key difference. A request counter is a single number, so atomic works perfectly. But an account with balance and pending fields needs both to change together, or readers see invalid data.

The BrokenAccount shows a common mistake. Each atomic operation is safe on its own, but the two operations together are not atomic. If balance starts at 100 and pending at 0, another goroutine might see balance=50 and pending=0 (total=50) instead of the correct total of 100.
CompareAndSwap: Building Lock-Free Structures
Sometimes Add, Store, and Swap aren't enough. What if you need to update a value only if it hasn't changed since you last read it? That's what CompareAndSwap (CAS) does.

CAS takes two things: the value you expect, and the new value you want. If the actual value matches your expected value, CAS updates it and returns true. If someone else changed it first, CAS does nothing and returns false. You can then retry with the new value.
This pattern is called optimistic concurrency: assume no conflict, try the operation, and retry if there was one. It's faster than locking when conflicts are rare.

content.code: Maximum: 100

content.text: Here's what happens when two goroutines try to update at the same time. Say maxSeen is 50, and goroutines with values 99 and 100 both read old=50. The first one to call CAS(50, 99) succeeds. The second calls CAS(50, 100), but maxSeen is now 99, not 50, so CAS fails. It loops, reads old=99, and CAS(99, 100) succeeds.
The retry loop is the key pattern. Read the current value, compute what you want to do, try CAS. If it fails, someone else made progress, so start over. This is how lock-free data structures work.

content.title: Memory Ordering Complexity
content.message: Atomic operations only guarantee atomicity of single values, not ordering between operations on different variables. If you need multiple values to be consistent, use a mutex. When in doubt, use a mutex. Correctness beats performance.

content.text: Atomic Flags: Shutdown Signaling

How do you tell worker goroutines to stop? You could use a channel, but for a simple yes/no signal, atomic.Bool is easier. One goroutine sets the flag to true, and all workers see it on their next check.
The pattern is simple: workers check the flag in their loop. When main wants them to stop, it sets the flag. Each worker finishes its current work, sees the flag is true, and exits cleanly.

Use atomic.Bool for simple on/off signals like shutdown flags, feature toggles, or circuit breakers. Use channels when you need to send data along with the signal, or when you need to wait for the signal with select.

content.text: Atomic operations are the fastest synchronization primitive, but they only work for single values. For more complex patterns like one-time initialization, condition variables, and concurrent maps, the sync package provides additional primitives covered in the next section.
Mutex protects shared data. WaitGroup waits for goroutines to finish. But some problems need more specialized tools. This section covers four of them.
sync.Once: One-Time Initialization

Sometimes you need to initialize something exactly once. A database connection, a configuration file, a logger. If 10 goroutines all try to initialize at the same time, you want only one to do the work. The rest should wait and use the result.
sync.Once does this. Call once.Do(fn) from any goroutine. The first call runs fn. All other calls, even from different goroutines, do nothing. They just return immediately.

sync.Once for Singleton Pattern
A singleton is an object that exists only once in your program. Database connections are a good example. You want one connection pool shared by all your code, not a new connection every time.

content.message: sync.Once is a one-shot mechanism. Once Do() has been called, subsequent calls do nothing, even with a different function. If you need retriable initialization, use sync.Mutex with a boolean flag instead.

content.text: sync.Cond: Condition Variables
Sometimes a goroutine needs to wait until something becomes true. A queue has items. A resource is available. A task is complete. You could check in a loop, but that wastes CPU.
sync.Cond lets goroutines sleep until another goroutine wakes them. Wait() puts a goroutine to sleep. Signal() wakes one sleeping goroutine. Broadcast() wakes all of them.

content.text: The consumer goroutine starts first but the queue is empty. It calls Wait() and goes to sleep. When the producer calls Put(), it adds an item and calls Signal(). This wakes the consumer, which takes the item and prints "Got: 1". This repeats for each item.

Why use a for loop instead of if? Imagine two consumers waiting. Signal() wakes one, but before it can grab the item, the other consumer wakes up too and grabs it first. The first consumer finds an empty queue and must wait again. The for loop handles this.
sync.Cond.Broadcast: Wake All Waiters
Signal() wakes one goroutine. Broadcast() wakes all of them. This is useful when a condition affects multiple waiters at once.

A barrier is a good example. Workers arrive at a barrier and wait. When the last worker arrives, everyone can proceed together. The last worker calls Broadcast() to wake all the waiting workers at once.

content.text: Worker 1 arrives first and waits. Worker 2 arrives and waits. Worker 3 arrives last. Since all 3 are now here (count == target), Worker 3 calls Broadcast(). This wakes Workers 1 and 2 at the same time. All three print "proceeding" and continue.
sync.Map: Concurrent Map
A regular Go map is not safe for concurrent use. If two goroutines read and write at the same time, your program crashes. sync.Map is a map that multiple goroutines can use safely.

But sync.Map is not always faster. It's optimized for two cases: keys that are written once and read many times, or goroutines that access different keys. For other patterns, use a regular map with RWMutex.

LoadAndDelete() removes a key and returns its value in one step. Range() lets you iterate over all entries.

content.text: sync.Pool: Object Reuse

Every time you create an object with new() or make(), Go allocates memory. When you're done, the garbage collector frees it. This takes time. If your program creates and throws away thousands of objects per second, it slows down.

sync.Pool solves this. Instead of throwing objects away, you put them back in the pool. Next time you need one, you get it from the pool instead of creating a new one. Get() returns an object from the pool. Put() adds one back. If the pool is empty, Get() calls New() to create a fresh object.

JSON Encoder Pool
A web server handles many requests. Each request needs a buffer to build the JSON response. Creating a new buffer for every request wastes memory. A pool lets you reuse buffers across requests.
When a request comes in, Get() gives you a buffer. You encode JSON into it, send the response, then Put() returns it to the pool. The next request uses the same buffer. No new allocation needed.

content.title: Reset Before Use
content.message: Always reset pooled objects after getting them from the pool. They may contain leftover data from the previous user. Call buf.Reset() for bytes.Buffer, or zero out struct fields manually.

content.text: x/sync/semaphore: Weighted Semaphore

Sometimes you need to limit how many goroutines can do something at once. A buffered channel works, but it's all-or-nothing: you either have access or you wait. A semaphore is more flexible. You can acquire 1 slot for a small task or 3 slots for a large task.

The golang.org/x/sync/semaphore package provides this. Create a semaphore with a total weight (like 10 slots). Each goroutine acquires some weight before starting and releases it when done. If not enough weight is available, Acquire() blocks until others release.

content.text: These primitives give you fine-grained control over synchronization. In the next section, we'll combine them with goroutines and channels to build worker pools, one of the most practical concurrency patterns for production systems.

Imagine you need to download 1,000 files. You could spawn 1,000 goroutines, but that would overwhelm the server and your network. A better approach: use 10 workers. Each worker downloads one file, then grabs the next. That is a worker pool. A worker pool is a fixed set of goroutines that pull jobs from a shared channel. Instead of one goroutine per task, you reuse a small team of workers. New jobs wait in line until a worker is free.
Why Limit Concurrency?

Spawning goroutines is cheap, but not free. Too many goroutines cause problems. Your database might only allow 100 connections. External APIs have rate limits. Each goroutine uses memory. Your CPU can only do so much at once. Worker pools let you control how many tasks run at the same time. Pick a number that matches your limits.

items.label: API Rate Limits
items.description: External APIs often limit to 100 req/sec. Worker pool prevents exceeding limits.

items.label: Database Connections
items.description: Connection pools typically have 20-100 connections. More workers waste time waiting.

items.label: Memory Pressure
items.description: Each goroutine uses ~2KB stack. 1M goroutines = 2GB just for stacks.

items.label: CPU Efficiency
items.description: More goroutines than CPU cores causes context switching overhead.

content.text: Basic Worker Pool Pattern

A worker pool has three components working together. First, a jobs channel acts as a queue where you send work items. Second, worker goroutines sit in a loop, waiting for jobs. When a job arrives, a worker grabs it, processes it, and sends the result to the third component: a results channel. The key insight is that workers use range to read from the jobs channel. This means they block when the channel is empty and automatically exit when you close it. The WaitGroup tracks how many workers are still running, so you know when all work is done.

When you run the code, all three workers start immediately and wait for jobs. As soon as jobs arrive, workers compete to grab them. The first three jobs go to workers 1, 2, and 3. When worker 1 finishes job 1, it immediately grabs job 4 while workers 2 and 3 are still busy. Meanwhile, main is reading from the results channel. Results may arrive out of order since workers finish at different times. After all 10 jobs complete, wg.Wait() returns in the background goroutine, which closes the results channel. This causes the range loop in main to exit, and the program ends.

content.text: Why Close Results in a Goroutine?

Main needs to do two things: read results from workers, and know when all workers are done. The problem is that wg.Wait() blocks until all workers finish. If main calls wg.Wait() before reading results, it stops and waits. But workers are trying to send results to main. With nobody reading, the results channel fills up and workers block too. Everyone is waiting, nobody is working. This is a deadlock. The fix is simple: run wg.Wait() in a separate goroutine. Now main can read results while the background goroutine waits. When all workers finish, the background goroutine closes the results channel, which tells main to stop reading.

content.title: Common Mistake: Deadlock
content.message: Do not call wg.Wait() in main before reading results. Main blocks waiting for workers. Workers block trying to send results. Nobody makes progress. Always use a background goroutine to wait and close the results channel.

content.text: Visualizing the Worker Pool

Picture a factory with three stations and a conveyor belt. Jobs arrive on the belt and wait in line. Each station (worker) picks up one job, processes it, and drops the result into an output bin. When a station finishes, it grabs the next job from the belt. The belt is your jobs channel, stations are worker goroutines, and the output bin is your results channel.

Think of a restaurant kitchen. Orders come in and wait on a ticket rail. A fixed number of cooks grab tickets and prepare dishes. More orders do not mean more cooks. The cooks you have work through the queue. In Go, the channel is the ticket rail. Goroutines are the cooks. Jobs wait in the channel buffer until a worker is free.
Using errgroup for Worker Pools

The basic pattern teaches you how worker pools work, but production code often uses the errgroup package from golang.org/x/sync. It handles WaitGroup for you and makes error handling easy. Call g.SetLimit(n) to set the maximum number of concurrent goroutines. Then call g.Go() for each task. If n goroutines are already running, g.Go() blocks until one finishes. When any goroutine returns an error, errgroup cancels the context and g.Wait() returns that error.

We have 6 URLs but only 3 can run at once. The first 3 start immediately. When one finishes, the next URL starts. Notice there are no channels or WaitGroup in this code. errgroup handles all of that internally. The context lets you cancel all goroutines if needed, and any error automatically stops the remaining work.

How many workers? It depends on your bottleneck. CPU-heavy tasks: use runtime.NumCPU() workers. More just adds overhead. I/O tasks like HTTP requests: workers mostly wait, so use 10x to 100x your CPU count. Memory-heavy tasks: divide available RAM by memory per task.

When your app shuts down, workers should finish their current jobs first. Use context cancellation to signal stop. Workers check ctx.Done() and exit after completing their task. Add a timeout so stuck workers do not block shutdown forever.
